seo.title: Interior Design Payment Schedule in Gurgaon: Stage by Stage
seo.description: How interior design payments work in Gurgaon: typical stage-wise percentages, what each payment should buy you, GST, retention and the red flags to avoid.

title: How Interior Design Payments Are Structured in Gurgaon: A Stage-by-Stage Breakdown
author: Shivam Kumar

featuredImage.alt: An interior designer reviewing floor plans and a payment schedule with homeowners

excerpt: A staged payment schedule matches your money to what your designer is actually spending, from drawings to factory orders to site work. See the 5 typical stages, a worked ₹30 lakh example, and the red flags to avoid.
keyTakeaways: Payments Follow Work, Not Dates — Each milestone should be tied to a checkable deliverable, not a date on a calendar.
Design Sign-Off Is the Biggest Payment — Typically 35–45%, released only once every room, finish and brand is named, since materials get ordered right after.
Never Pay More Than Half Before Sign-Off — Paying for materials that haven't been chosen yet is the single biggest payment-schedule risk.

contentHtml:
Most turnkey interior projects in Gurgaon are paid in 4–5 milestones, not as one lump sum. A common pattern is 10% at booking, 40% at design sign-off, 30% mid-execution, 15% at installation and 5% at handover. Each payment should be tied to something you can see and check, and a small final amount should be held back until every snag is fixed. GST at 18% is usually charged on top of each instalment.

Key takeaways

  • Payments should follow work completed, not dates on a calendar.
  • The biggest payment usually comes at design sign-off, because that is when the designer orders materials and starts factory production.
  • Never pay more than about half the project value before the design is final and signed.
  • Keep 5–10% back until handover and snag closure. It is your strongest lever for a clean finish.
  • Every change after sign-off should come as a written variation with its cost, added to the next milestone.

Why interior payments are split into stages

Interior work is not like buying a sofa. Your designer spends money long before anything reaches your flat: drawings and 3D views, then plywood, laminates, hardware and factory time for the kitchen and wardrobes, then carpenters, electricians and painters on site. A staged payment schedule matches your money to that spending.

It protects both sides. The firm isn't funding your project out of its own pocket, and you are never far ahead of the work that has actually been done. If something goes wrong in the middle, you have paid for what exists, not for what was promised. For how that spending maps to time, see our guide to the turnkey interior project timeline.

The exact percentages vary from firm to firm. What should not vary is the principle: each payment is released when a clear, checkable milestone is complete.

The 5 payment stages of a turnkey project

Here is the structure most full-home turnkey projects in Gurgaon follow, with the typical share at each stage and what you should have in hand before you pay.

StageTypical shareWhen it is paidWhat you should get first
1. Booking & design start5–10%After you accept the proposalSigned agreement, scope, estimated budget, timeline
2. Design sign-off & order35–45%When you approve final designsFinal 2D drawings, 3D views, material and finish list, itemised quote
3. Mid-execution25–30%When civil, electrical and ceiling work is done, or materials reach siteSite photos or a visit; material delivery matched to the spec sheet
4. Installation complete10–15%When kitchen, wardrobes and furniture are installedWalkthrough; snag list prepared and shared
5. Handover5–10%After snags are fixed and the home is cleanedSnag closure, warranty documents, care guide, final invoice

Percentages are typical market ranges, not a fixed rule. Your contract should state the exact split.

Stage 1: Booking and design kick-off (5–10%)

This payment starts the design work. It pays for measurements, layout planning, concept boards and the first rounds of 3D views. Many firms adjust this amount against the total project value, so it is not an extra cost. Ask whether it is refundable if you decide not to go ahead after the concept stage. Some firms refund part of it; most keep it as a design fee. For what this stage should actually cover, see our guide to what's included in a full-home interior package.

Stage 2: Design sign-off and order placement (35–45%)

This is the largest single payment, and for a good reason. Once you approve the final drawings and finishes, the firm places orders for boards, laminates, veneers, hardware, stone and lighting, and books factory time for modular units. Much of that money leaves the firm's account within days.

Because this payment is big, it is also where you should be most careful. Do not release it until the design is truly final: every room, every elevation, every finish and brand named. A vague "premium laminate" on a quote is how disputes start later. Our guide on how to compare and negotiate interior design quotations covers what an itemised quote should actually name.

Stage 3: Mid-execution (25–30%)

This payment funds the main site work. It is usually released when the "hidden" work is done: civil changes, electrical and plumbing points, false ceiling framing and wall preparation. Some firms tie it to material delivery instead. Either way, you should be able to see the progress, either on a site visit or through dated photos.

This is the right moment to check that what arrived matches what you approved, such as board grade, laminate codes and hardware brands, before it is fixed into the walls.

Stage 4: Installation complete (10–15%)

Paid once the kitchen, wardrobes, panelling and loose furniture are installed and the home looks nearly finished. Before releasing it, walk through every room with your designer and agree on a written snag list: chipped edges, misaligned shutters, paint touch-ups, loose handles, lights not working.

Stage 5: Handover (5–10%)

The last payment is your retention. Release it only when every snag on the list is closed, the site is cleaned, and you have the warranty papers, care instructions and final tax invoice. A firm that is confident in its finishing won't object to this. It is standard practice.

A worked example: ₹30 lakh turnkey 3BHK

To make the numbers real, here is how a ₹30 lakh (before GST) full-home turnkey project might be paid using a 10/40/30/15/5 split. For how this figure compares across home sizes, see our interior design cost guide for Gurgaon.

StageShareAmount (₹)GST @18% (₹)Total payable (₹)
Booking & design start10%3,00,00054,0003,54,000
Design sign-off & order40%12,00,0002,16,00014,16,000
Mid-execution30%9,00,0001,62,00010,62,000
Installation complete15%4,50,00081,0005,31,000
Handover5%1,50,00027,0001,77,000
Total100%30,00,0005,40,00035,40,000

The GST line is the one many homeowners forget. On this project it adds ₹5.4 lakh. Always ask whether a quote is "inclusive" or "plus GST", and plan your cash flow around the total payable, not the headline number. Our guide to hidden costs of interior design covers the other extras that catch homeowners out.

How payment structures differ by service type

Not every interior project is a full turnkey build. The payment pattern shifts depending on what you are buying.

Service typeHow it is usually paidWhy
Full-home turnkey4–5 milestones, as aboveSpending is spread across design, materials and months of site work
Design-only (you hire your own contractor)Fee of a % of project value or a rate per sq ft, paid in 2–3 parts: advance, design approval, final drawingsYou are paying for drawings and advice, not materials
Modular kitchen or wardrobes onlyHigher upfront share, often 50–60% at order, balance before dispatch or at installationUnits are factory-made to your size and cannot be resold
Renovation of an older homeMilestones plus a contingency, often 10%, for surprises after demolitionOld wiring, plumbing and seepage are only found once walls are opened

For a fuller comparison of how these arrangements work, see our guide to turnkey vs traditional interior design.

Red flags in a payment schedule

A payment schedule tells you a lot about how a firm works. Be cautious if you see any of these:

  • More than 50% before design sign-off. You would be paying for materials that haven't been chosen yet.
  • Payments tied to dates, not work. "30% in week 6" means you pay even if the site is behind.
  • 100% before installation. You lose all leverage over finishing and snags.
  • Cash payments or no proper invoice. You lose your paper trail, warranty claims get harder, and GST compliance becomes unclear.
  • Changes agreed verbally. Unrecorded changes are the most common reason final bills don't match the quote.

Our guide to questions to ask your interior designer covers what to ask before you sign anything.

How to protect yourself at every stage

  1. Get the payment schedule written into the contract, with the milestone for each payment clearly defined.
  2. Pay by bank transfer, UPI or cheque, and get a receipt or tax invoice for every instalment.
  3. Ask for an itemised quote with brands and grades before the sign-off payment.
  4. Record every change as a variation order with its cost and time impact, signed by both sides.
  5. Visit the site, or ask for dated photos, before each payment.
  6. Hold back the final 5–10% until the snag list is closed and warranties are in your hands.

If you would rather spread the cost, some firms offer financing. See our guide to no-cost EMI for interior design in Gurgaon.

faqs.question: What is the usual payment schedule for interior design in Gurgaon?
faqs.answer: Most turnkey projects are paid in 4–5 stages. A common split is 10% at booking, 40% at design sign-off, 30% mid-execution, 15% when installation is complete and 5% at handover. Exact percentages vary by firm and should be written into your contract.

faqs.question: How much advance should I pay an interior designer?
faqs.answer: A booking advance of 5–10% of the project value is typical to start design work. Be cautious about paying more than about half the project value before the final design is approved and signed.

faqs.question: Why is the design sign-off payment so large?
faqs.answer: Because that is when the firm orders materials and books factory production for modular kitchens and wardrobes. Much of the project's material cost is spent right after you approve the design.

faqs.question: Is GST charged on interior design payments?
faqs.answer: Yes. Interior design services and interior works contracts are generally taxed at 18% GST. It is usually charged on each instalment, so check whether your quote is inclusive or exclusive of GST.

faqs.question: Should I keep a retention amount until handover?
faqs.answer: Yes. Holding back 5–10% until the snag list is closed and you have warranty documents is standard practice and gives you leverage to get the finishing right.

faqs.question: Why do modular kitchen companies ask for 50% or more upfront?
faqs.answer: Modular units are factory-made to your exact measurements and can't be reused for another home, so suppliers ask for a larger share at order to cover production.

faqs.question: What happens to payments if I change the design midway?
faqs.answer: Changes after sign-off should be issued as written variation orders that show the extra cost and any delay. The amount is usually added to the next milestone payment. Changes after materials are ordered or civil work begins can cost more.
